63: Priority date and antedating: whether CE's fabrication of the prototype inured to Charrat's benefit, and whether his conception was adequately corroborated so that the claims antedate the Sears reference
Accordingly, we reverse the Board's determination relating to Charrat's conception, and determine that CE's fabrication of the prototype inured to Charrat's benefit.
390: Priority date of the Raymond reference: the Board found Dynamic failed to prove Raymond was entitled to its February 15, 2000 provisional date, so Raymond's effective date is its May 5, 2000 filing date. The court affirmed, holding the provisional lacked written description support for the Raymond claims and that the petitioner bears the burden of production and persuasion on the earlier date.
Nowhere, however, does Dynamic demonstrate support in the Raymond provisional application for the claims of the Raymond patent.
539: On-sale bar under §102(b): whether pre-critical-date sale of services producing the product-by-process constituted a commercial offer for sale, invalidating the claims
we find that the district court clearly erred in finding the Ben Venue sale of services did not constitute a commercial sale.
540: Experimental use exception to the on-sale bar: whether the Ben Venue batches were prepared primarily for experimental purposes and thus not barred
The district court also clearly erred in finding that the experimental use doctrine bars the application of the onsale bar to the Ben Venue batches.
541: Ready for patenting prong of the on-sale bar: whether the invention was reduced to practice or described sufficiently before the critical date
Thus, the district court did not clearly err in finding the invention was ready for patenting.
720: Prior-art status under the public use bar: whether the SRI TerraVision demonstrations and source code distribution before the December 17, 1995 critical date were public uses that were ready for patenting and discernable to the public, so as to qualify as prior art.

Lau's testimony regarding his demonstrations at these conferences and his provision of source code to individuals at Art+Com constitutes substantial evidence that SRI TerraVision was "ready for patenting."
951: On-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b): whether Merck's September 9, 1998 fax was a commercial offer for sale of claimed MTHF before the critical date, invalidating claim 4 of the '168 patent.
Because Merck's September 9, 1998, offer to sell MTHF was a premature commercial exploitation of its invention, claim 4 of the '168 patent is invalid under the on-sale bar.
1171: Prior-art status under the on-sale bar: whether the invention was ready for patenting before the critical date (reduction to practice), so the on-sale bar applies; the court held the invention was reduced to practice and ready for patenting before January 30, 2002.
We conclude that the invention was reduced to practice and therefore was ready for patenting before the critical date.
1194: Novartis and Schering PCT applications not prior art under pre-AIA 102(e)(1) because provisional applications lacked written description support; JMOL of non-obviousness affirmed on that basis.
Because the district court properly excluded Novartis and Schering under Dynamic Drinkware, the court’s grant of JMOL of non-obviousness was proper.
1241: Prior-art status and earlier invention date: whether REG proved conception before Dindi's June 13, 2008 filing date so Dindi is not prior art; court reversed the Board's conception finding and vacated Dindi anticipation of claims 2 and 5.
We reverse the Board's finding that REG failed to establish conception of the invention prior to Dindi's filing date of June 13, 2008.
1394: Priority date: whether the '720, '181 and '105 patents are entitled to the January 19, 2000 filing date via §120 continuation chain (same-day filing before patenting), so WO '109 publication is not prior art
1508: Prior-art status: whether TransWeb's 1997 expo distribution of plasma-fluorinated material was a public use qualifying as prior art; the court found the testimony sufficiently corroborated.
As such, we find no clear error in the district court's determination that Mr. Ogale's testimony was sufficiently corroborated.
1844: Whether the Ratsimor report was a printed publication (publicly accessible prior art) under pre-AIA 102(b)
we agree with the Board that Groupon failed to carry its burden of proving public accessibility of the Ratsimor Reference.
1914: Whether reference Fan (US 2002/0172946) qualifies as prior art to the '794 patent claims; Board held Fan is not prior art and the court affirmed.
Because the Board did not err in determining that Fan is not prior art and did not abuse its discretion in denying Ariosa's request for rehearing, we affirm the Board's decision.
2006: Whether the '411 patent qualifies as prior art to the ISV patents under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(e) and 103(c).
Accordingly, the '411 patent qualifies as prior art to the ISV patents under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(e) and 103(c) (2006).
2082: Priority date: whether the '915 patent is entitled to the May 1989 filing date of the '072 application, making Engelmann not prior art.
Because the '072 application provides an adequate written description of the protein claimed in Abbott's '915 patent, the '915 patent benefits from the priority date of the '072 application.
2140: Public use bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b): whether third-party cultivation of unreleased grape varieties (Ludy cousins) was accessible to the public and thus invalidating prior art. Court held no invalidating public use, so the plant patents' critical-date prior-art challenge failed.
The district court found that the actions of those individuals did not constitute a public use of the two plant varieties and therefore rejected the plaintiffs' challenge to the patents. We affirm.
2174: Whether Beachy's applications are entitled to the earlier priority date of the benefit applications, so that Beachy is the senior party and Taş's '078 patent is later.

We therefore affirm the PTAB's denial of Taş's preliminary motions regarding no interference-in-fact and lack of written description and enablement for the Counts of the '926 and '949 interferences and the claims of the '121 and '934 applications.
2368: Whether PST antedated JP '551 by showing conception plus reasonable diligence in reducing to practice; Board applied an overly exacting continuous-diligence standard and erred in disregarding attorney Heslin's activities; decision vacated and remanded
The standard demanded by the Board is too exacting and in conflict with our precedent.
2431: Whether the disputed references (rock carvings, engraved signage, Prussian Blue) are analogous prior art; the court held the jury could find them not analogous, so only the stipulated prior art counts.

Because the jury's presumed finding that the disputed references are not analogous is supported by substantial evidence, the only references within the scope of the prior art are the stipulated prior art.
2464: Whether Fey is analogous art (prior art status of reference) for claims 7, 35-40, 42-47
The Board properly found that Fey is reasonably pertinent to the problem at hand
2472: Whether applicants antedated the Evans reference (effective date Dec. 23, 2002) under Rule 131 by showing actual reduction to practice or conception plus diligence; court held Evans remains prior art.
Thus the Evans publication remains as a reference.
2651: Entitlement to the October 2002 provisional priority date; the court held the '903 patent lacks adequate written description in the provisional, so it is not entitled to that date.
we conclude on the merits that the '903 patent is not entitled to the priority date of the provisional application because of a lack of adequate written description.
2928: Prior conception and earlier priority date: the Board's finding that IV did not prove prior conception before the critical date was vacated because the Board misapplied the rule of reason to corroboration for both the LAN routing and stand-alone system limitations, so the claims may be entitled to the earlier conception date.
we vacate the Board's finding of no prior conception, and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
3022: On-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b): whether MedCo's contract manufacturing transactions with Ben Venue and stockpiling constituted a commercial sale of the claimed product, making it prior art. The en banc court held no invalidating commercial sale occurred and affirmed the district court's ruling that the asserted claims were not invalid under the on-sale bar.
We conclude, moreover, that no such invalidating commercial sale occurred in this case.
3206: Whether Campbell '558 qualifies as 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art, given the inventor declaration claiming sole invention by a common inventive entity
The Board did not err in holding Campbell ’558 is § 102(e) prior art.
3403: Prior-art status and priority date: whether the SVS system was reduced to practice before the July 10, 1997 filing date and qualifies as prior art, and whether Alexsam proved an earlier conception/reduction to practice date for the patents.
For these reasons, the jury lacked substantial evidence to find the SVS system did not anticipate the patents-in-suit.
3474: Physio-Control 510(k) application not sufficiently publicly accessible to be a printed publication prior art; exclusion affirmed
the district court did not abuse its discretion in excluding this evidence from the invalidity trial.
3515: Whether the '598 patent is entitled to the earlier priority date of the '650 parent application; Board found the interface module lacked written-description support there, so the later date applies.
We conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board’s written-description-based determination that the ’598 patent is not entitled to the ’650 application’s priority date.
3543: Prior-art status and priority date: Netac attempted to swear behind three primary references; the court agreed with the Board that Netac could not antedate them and that they were properly considered prior art.
We thus agree with the Board that Netac cannot antedate any of the three primary references and that they were properly considered prior art.
3664: Claims of the '288 patent entitled to a 2006 priority date (supported by the parent application) rather than a 2013 date, so the on-sale bar based on 2010 sales did not raise a substantial invalidity question.
The district court did not err in determining that the claims of the '288 patent are supported by the written description in the parent application, which was filed in 2006.
3671: Whether the '216 patent is entitled to the earlier priority date of the Australian provisional applications; Board held no, because the provisionals do not disclose the summation algorithm structure for the generating means term.
we agree with the Board that the '216 patent may not claim priority to the Australian provisionals.
3859: Priority date: Auris (junior party) not entitled to the benefit of its 2005 PCT filing date or any effective filing date before June 2014, so Auris's patent post-dates Otonomy's publication and the Board's priority judgment was reversed.
We reverse the Board's accorded benefit decision and find that Auris is not entitled to an effective filing date before June 2014.
3886: Whether the Jentschel article (May/June 1996 German journal issue) was publicly accessible and thus qualifies as a printed publication prior art reference before Ericsson's earliest asserted filing date.
Substantial evidence supports the Board's ruling that Jentschel was accessible to the public in the May/June 1996 period.
3919: Whether the GoPro Catalog (2009 dealer-show distribution) qualifies as a printed publication and thus prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b); the court held it was publicly accessible prior art.
we conclude that GoPro met its burden to show that its catalog is a printed publication under § 102(b).
3950: Whether the ABT Catalog qualifies as a pre-critical-date printed publication (public accessibility and corroboration of the March 2003 date); Board found it prior art and the court affirmed.
We agree with Instradent that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the ABT Catalog was publicly accessible prior to the critical date.
4061: Whether Bertin qualifies as prior art, i.e., whether the inventors antedated Bertin by an earlier actual reduction to practice; court held Raytheon failed to antedate
we affirm the Board’s determination that Raytheon failed to antedate Bertin, and that Bertin also renders appealed claims 5 and 13 of the ’678 patent obvious.
4326: Whether the Continuation Patents are entitled to the earlier priority date of the '126 patent; held not entitled because the '300 patent broke the chain of priority and the '126 patent disclaimed fixed rear soles, so Nike's prior sales are prior art under the on-sale bar.
the Continuation Patents cannot claim priority to the '126 patent for claims covering a conventional fixed rear sole because the chain of priority was broken by the '300 patent.
4359: Whether the 'bed in a box' website qualifies as prior art given a factual dispute over whether it predated the priority date; court held the dispute precludes reliance on it at summary judgment.
At best, the disputed fact regarding the publication date of the "bed in a box" reference precludes reliance on that reference for purposes of summary judgment.
4374: Whether Emanuel PCT is prior art or whether the '359 patent is entitled to its earlier priority date based on written description support for the claimed light guide permanently affixed in the first channel
We affirm the Board's finding that Emanuel PCT provides written description support for claims 1–3 and 5–7 of the '359 patent and that the '359 patent is entitled to claim priority to Emanuel PCT.
4389: On-sale bar (prior-art status under pre-AIA §102(b)): grant of summary judgment rejecting the on-sale bar defense vacated because the record is insufficiently developed; no ruling on whether the bar applies.
We conclude that the district court erred in granting summary judgment because the record is not sufficient to grant summary judgment for either side.
4474: Whether the Bradford book is a printed publication and thus prior art against the '997 patent (publicly accessible before the May 9, 2012 priority date).
We affirm the Board's ruling that Bradford is prior art against the '997 patent.
4563: Whether RFC 2401 qualifies as a printed publication (prior art) as of November 1998, decided through collateral estoppel from a prior Rule 36 judgment and alternatively on the merits.
Accordingly, by affirming all seven of the Board's decisions, this court in VirnetX I necessarily found that RFC 2401 was a printed publication.
4576: Prior-art status of the CS-1762 device: testimony that firmware existed in 2006 did not prove it predated the July 24, 2006 critical date, so the CS-1762 reference was not shown to be prior art.

With a critical date of July 24, 2006, testimony that the firmware running on the CS-1762 device existed in 2006 alone is not enough to support the jury's finding that the firmware pre-dated the critical date and thus qualifies as prior art.
4672: Prior-art status and priority date: substantial evidence supported the inventors' conception and reduction to practice before the May 2011 public use of the 3G7 product, so 3G7 is not prior art.

Therefore, substantial evidence supports the inventors' story of a conception date and reduction to practice before the May 17, 2011 public use date of 3G7, and, therefore, 3G7 is not anticipatory prior art.
4710: Prior-art status and earlier date: inventors' August 1998 prototype reduced to practice claims 1, 2, 9-11 and 18 before Yasushi's November 1998 date, so Yasushi is not prior art to those claims.
We affirm the Board’s holding that challenged claims 1, 2, 9–11, and 18 were reduced to practice prior to November 1998.
4711: Prior-art status and later date: the record does not show reduction to practice before Yasushi's date for claims 3, 12, 19 and 20, so Yasushi remains prior art to those claims.
We reverse the Board’s holding that challenged claims 3, 12, 19, and 20 were reduced to practice prior to November 1998.
4730: On-sale bar (prior-art status): the July 2003 proposal was a pre-critical-date offer for sale and the invention was ready for patenting; the court found no abuse of discretion in applying the on-sale bar.
The District Court did not abuse its discretion in determining that the claimed invention was the subject of an offer for sale in the summer of 2003.
4794: Priority date: Microspherix patents entitled to the Microspherix provisional date, and Zamora not entitled to its provisional date, so Zamora is not prior art under §102(e).
On this record, we are not persuaded that Zamora is supported by its provisional.
5027: Whether the WD4 reference was publicly accessible (prior art) via the JCT-VC and MPEG websites; the Board's finding that it was not accessible there was affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.

Samsung did not offer evidence, apart from the speculation of Mr. Bross, that a person of ordinary skill, exercising reasonable diligence, would have located the JCT-VC website or even known to look for it.
5028: Whether the October 2011 emailing of WD4 to the JCT-VC listserv made it publicly accessible prior art; the Board applied the wrong legal standard (access versus accessibility), so the finding was vacated and remanded.

Accordingly, we vacate the Board's finding that Mr. Bross's email did not make the WD4 reference publicly accessible and remand so that the Board can consider this issue after applying the correct legal standard.
5030: Alternative holding that, even if not waived, distribution at the Torino and Geneva meetings would not make WD4 prior art because WD4 was created after Torino and Geneva occurred after the critical date.
The WD4 reference was not created until after the Torino meeting.
5034: Whether the Lin technical report is a printed publication under §102(a) (public accessibility); the Board's finding that Lin is not prior art was affirmed, favoring the patent owner.
The Board did not err in concluding Lin is not a printed publication.
5048: Effective filing date and on-sale bar: claims 1 and 6 entitled to the February 4, 2003 earlier filing date, so the on-sale bar does not invalidate them; denial of LNC's summary judgment of invalidity affirmed.
For the foregoing reasons, the district court’s order denying LNC’s motion for summary judgment of invalidity is affirmed.
5071: Whether Ultraproof's copyright registrations show the designs were described in a printed publication before the effective filing date under §102(a); the court agreed a genuine dispute exists on the publication date, so the ground was rejected at summary judgment.
The district court thus denied this ground of invalidity at the summary judgment phase. We agree with the district court and thus reject this alternative ground.
5169: Whether the ’054 patent qualifies as §102(e) prior art because the anticipating embodiment was jointly invented by King and Schwarz, so it is 'by another'
Thus, the anticipating embodiment was the joint invention of King and Schwarz, an inventive entity different from that of the ’310 patent, and the ’054 patent is prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102(e).
5175: Prior-art status and priority date for the '053 patent: whether ATI antedated the Stuttard, Moreton and Lindholm references by proving conception plus reasonably continuous diligence to constructive reduction to practice. The court held the PTAB applied the wrong diligence standard and that diligence was shown, so the references are antedated.
We conclude that the PTAB applied the wrong legal standard for diligence.
5176: Prior-art status and priority date for the '871 patent: whether ATI antedated Lindholm through diligence to constructive reduction to practice. The court held the PTAB's diligence ruling was in error and reversed it.
The Board's rulings as to diligence are in error, in all three patents, for the same reasons. These rulings are reversed.
5177: Prior-art status and priority date for the '369 patent: whether ATI antedated Lindholm through diligence to constructive reduction to practice. The court held the PTAB's diligence ruling was in error and reversed it.
The Board erred in holding that diligence had not been shown for the three Unified Shader Patents.
5264: Whether the ACA materials (FDA advisory committee materials accessed via Federal Register notice hyperlink) were publicly accessible and qualify as prior art printed publications under pre-AIA §102(b).

we hold that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the ACA materials were publicly accessible to persons of ordinary skill exercising reasonable diligence before the critical date of the patents in suit.
5659: Whether the '455 PCT publication is prior art to the electrical claims, which turns on whether the '817 application incorporates Severinsky and so gives the claims an earlier priority date; court held Severinsky is incorporated in its entirety and vacated the obviousness finding, remanding on written description.

When read in context, the passage makes clear that it incorporates the entire Severinsky document into the '817 application, but applies only some of the specific features of Severinsky's invention disclosed in that document to the '817 application's invention.
5761: Public use bar under pre-AIA 102(b): the court held substantial evidence supported the jury's finding that Polara's Fullerton prototype testing was experimental use, so the claims were not invalidated by public use.
We agree with Polara that substantial evidence supports the jury's finding of experimental use that negates application of the public use bar.
5790: Section 102(a) prior knowledge or use: secret, confidential knowledge and use by a third party is not accessible to the public and is not prior art; genuine fact issues remain for trial.

Prior knowledge or use that is not accessible to the public "upon reasonable inquiry," Gayler, 51 U.S. (10 How.) at 497, confers no benefit on the public, and thus does not suffice as a defense under § 102(a).
5791: Section 102(b) public-use bar: rejected a per se rule that a third party's secret commercial use bars another inventor; genuine fact issues preclude summary judgment on public use.
SNF's second contention—that a third party's commercial exploitation of a secret process creates a per se public-use bar to another inventor—is simply wrong.
5792: Section 102(b) on-sale bar: the Sanyo-Celanese license, technical assistance, and the Hoechst acquisition did not constitute a sale of the claimed process, so no on-sale bar applies.
We reverse the district court's decision and hold that the '329 patent claims are not invalid under the on-sale bar of § 102(b).
5958: Priority date of the '150 patent: the '902 provisional application adequately supports the claims, so the '150 patent is entitled to the earlier filing date (written-description-based priority question).
We affirm the district court’s holding that the ’150 patent is entitled to the priority date of the ’902 application.
6016: Boyd (April 1, 2002 filing) held not prior art because Janisch's invention was conceived before that date and reasonably diligently reduced to practice, so the patents antedate Boyd; Board's contrary ruling reversed.
There being no dispute about conception before April 2002, we hold that Mr. Janisch's invention antedated Boyd.
6084: Effective filing date and prior-art status: the '115 Patent is entitled only to the November 24, 2003 date of the '838 Patent, so the Franco PCT published in March 2001 is prior art; incorporation by reference cannot supply a §120 specific reference.

Because the ’115 Patent contains the statutorily-required specific reference under § 120 and regulation 1.78 to the ’838 Patent, the Board correctly concluded that the ’115 Patent’s effective filing date is November 24, 2003, the filing date of the ’838 Patent.
6239: Section 102(b) public-use and on-sale bars against the '358 patent: the court held the invention was not ready for patenting before the critical date and that the pre-critical-date surgeries were experimental use, so the bars did not invalidate the claims.
The jury could reasonably find facts that support rejection of Medtronic's contention that Dr. Barry's '358 invention was ready for patenting before December 30, 2003.
6240: Section 102(g) prior-invention challenge to both patents: the court upheld the jury finding that Dr. Lenke did not reduce the claimed inventions to practice before Dr. Barry did, so Barry's earlier date controls.

We uphold the jury's rejection of Medtronic's § 102(g) challenge because there is substantial evidence to support a finding that Dr. Lenke did not reduce the claimed inventions to practice before February 2006, after Dr. Barry did so (for both patents at issue here).
6324: Whether Chen '393 qualifies as prior art, i.e., whether Kolcraft antedated it by showing prior conception of the design patents' claimed inventions through corroborated inventor testimony.
Kolcraft failed to independently corroborate inventor testimony of prior conception.
6377: Public use under pre-AIA 102(a) of Neupro patches containing Form II rotigotine before the '414 priority date, invalidating the '414 claims.
The district court reasonably found that a patient in the United States used Neupro patches that contained Form II rotigotine before November 28, 2007
6446: Priority: whether Wyoming is entitled to the benefit of the earlier filing dates of its priority applications, so that Wyoming is senior party over Chevron's later conception and diligence date.
We therefore affirm the Board's judgment in the interference in favor of Wyoming.
6588: Whether GoPro's 2009 sales catalog was a printed publication and thus prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), based on its distribution at a dealer trade show; the court held it was prior art and vacated the Board's no-printed-publication finding.
we conclude that GoPro met its burden to show that its catalog is a printed publication under § 102(b).
6881: Prior-art status and priority date: whether the Distribution Agreement was a commercial offer for sale triggering the on-sale bar under §102(b) before the critical date.

Because the district court erred in concluding that the Distribution Agreement was not a commercial offer for sale, we reverse and remand for the court to determine whether the offer to sell covered the patented invention.
6882: Prior-art status: invention was ready for patenting before the critical date, so the on-sale bar's second prong is satisfied.
The district court correctly determined that the invention was ready for patenting before the critical date.
6948: Whether the 61 prior frac jobs were experimental rather than prior commercial sales/public uses qualifying under the on-sale bar
The district court did not clearly err in finding that Mr. Hefley's 61 prior commercial sales and public uses were not experimental.
7002: Whether the IsoMed guide qualifies as a printed publication (prior art under pre-AIA 102(b)); Board determination vacated and remanded for factfinding, so no final prior-art ruling.
we vacate the Board's determination that IsoMed qualifies as a printed publication and remand for additional factfinding on this score.
7058: Priority date challenge to the ʼ422 patent: the Board's determination that the claims were not entitled to the earlier priority date of the parent application, so the reference counts as prior art, affirmed by incorporation of the companion opinion.
Regarding the merits of this appeal, we affirm the Board's final determination and its denial of NAI's request for rehearing for the reasons stated in our companion opinion.
7129: Field of endeavor: whether Kotliar is analogous prior art because it is outside the same field of endeavor as the '752 patent. The court held the Board's finding that Kotliar is not in the same field was supported by substantial evidence.
We therefore conclude that the Board's determination under the field of endeavor test is supported by substantial evidence.
7130: Reasonably pertinent test: whether Kotliar is analogous prior art under the reasonably pertinent test. The court held the Board erred by refusing to consider record evidence of the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill, and vacated the reversal of the examiner's rejection.
We accordingly vacate the Board's reversal of the examiner's rejection and remand for the Board to reconsider its analogous art determination.
7156: Priority date under 35 U.S.C. 120: the ʼ381 patent's claims are not entitled to the filing date of the first application because the intervening fifth application's benefit claim was deleted, so the priority claim was defective from the start.

The Board, therefore, did not err in determining that the ʼ381 patent was not entitled to claim the benefit of the filing date of the first application under § 120, as the priority claim in the ʼ381 patent was defective from the start.
7216: Prior conception to swear behind Ahy reference: GAS failed to establish prior conception of the claimed inventions before Ahy's filing date, so Ahy remains prior art.
We agree with the Board that the conclusory assertions in GAS's patent owner response are insufficient to meet GAS's burden of establishing prior conception.
7320: Priority date: the Asserted Claims are not entitled to the February 5, 2009 effective filing date, so intervening prior art applies.
the Patents-in-Suit cannot claim priority from the 2009 Application
7337: Whether Joshi qualifies as prior art under 102(e), i.e., whether the '376 patent is entitled to an earlier date based on the '534 provisional
we hold that Joshi qualifies as prior art and that the Board permissibly relied on Joshi in all three grounds of the Board's obviousness analysis.
7402: Priority date: the district court found claim 10 of the '184 patent not entitled to priority to the parent application because the '1 to 20 minutes daily' limitation lacked written description support there; the Federal Circuit affirmed that the challenger had adequately shown the claim was not entitled to the earlier date.

The issue on appeal is thus whether Propel presented sufficient evidence that claim 10 was not entitled to claim priority to the parent application for the district court to place the burden on OrthoAccel to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the invalidity issue at trial.
7536: Priority date of claim 10 of the '309 patent via provisional applications, so the Pan article is not prior art; affirmed.
We therefore affirm the district court's ruling that claim 10 of the '309 patent is not anticipated by the Pan article.
7544: Whether the Sourcefire user guide qualifies as a printed publication and thus as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 311(b)/102.
We rely on our discussion in 20-1635 Decision to affirm the Board's ruling as to Sourcefire's qualification as a printed publication here.
7659: Ruling that prior Federal Circuit decision in Computer Packages did not address eligibility of the '437 patent; PTO allowance and presumption of validity do not establish eligibility (not prior-art issue, so this entry is dropped in favor of X99-free coding)
The district court concluded it was not bound by PTO's decisions and the agency's allowance of the '437 patent did not dictate the eligibility analysis.
7689: Prior-art status of the '096 publication under pre-AIA 102(a); district court found it prior art
We see no error in the district court's finding that the '096 publication is prior art.
7742: Priority date of claims 1 and 15 of the '101 patent: whether the '515 provisional application (March 20, 2002) supports an earlier date through inherent disclosure of crystalline Form B; court held claims entitled to the earlier date.

We agree with Amgen that the district court did not clearly err in finding that claims 1 and 15 of the '101 patent were entitled to the March 2002 priority date (i.e., the filing date of the '515 provisional application).
7774: Whether applicant admitted prior art (AAPA) in the challenged patent qualifies as prior art consisting of patents or printed publications under 35 U.S.C. 311(b) and may form the basis of an IPR ground. Held it does not qualify.
We agree with Qualcomm and the PTO that the "patents or printed publications" that form the "basis" of a ground for inter partes review must themselves be prior art to the challenged patent.
7843: On-sale bar: the Board found that an email from the patent owner offered an embodiment of the design claim for sale more than a year before the priority date, making the claim unpatentable under the on-sale bar; the court found the on-sale determination supported and affirmed.
The Board found that an email sent by patent owner Raffel offered for sale an embodiment of the claim in small quantities on-demand over a year before the priority date of the patent.
8113: Prior-art status: whether Weber's commercial operating manuals were publicly accessible and qualify as printed publications under pre-AIA 102(b).
We thus reverse the Board’s finding that Weber’s operating manuals do not qualify as printed publications.
8167: Whether the incorporated 2007 provisional application (’394 provisional) became publicly available through the published PCT application and so qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(b), given 37 C.F.R. 1.14 and the MPEP.
Under the MPEP, then, the ’394 provisional application became publicly available when the ’756 PCT was published.
8251: Whether Itou qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e); the challenged patents were antedated by showing actual reduction to practice before the critical date, with corroboration of inventor testimony and the intended-purpose and testing analysis.

Because we find the Board's determination of actual reduction prior to the critical date supported by substantial evidence, we affirm the Board's finding that Itou does not qualify as prior art to the challenged patents under 35 U.S.C. § 102(e).
8277: On-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b): whether the January 8, 1999 pre-critical-date letter was a commercial offer for sale of the claimed design, making the design D'839 patent invalid as prior art.
we agree with MedComp that the January 8, 1999 letter was a commercial offer for sale of the claimed design.
8355: Prior-art status: whether the Aurora device at AAGL 2009 was prior art under the public use bar and ready for patenting before the critical date.
We conclude that the district court correctly determined that the Aurora device was ready for patenting.
8398: Whether Finkelstein is analogous art (prior art) for the obviousness determination; substantial evidence supports Board's finding that Finkelstein is analogous art.
We conclude that there was substantial evidence supporting the Board's finding that Finkelstein is analogous art.
8454: Whether the ’779 patent specification's characterization of sucker-rod pumps and their components as conventional may be used as an admission of what was known in the art (prior-art status) in the anticipation and obviousness analysis; the court held the Board did not err in accepting it.
The Board did not err by accepting the specification's own assertions of what is well known in the art.
8536: Prior-art status and priority date: whether the ’830 claims are entitled to the earlier NP2/P1 filing dates or are limited to the March 28, 2014 date, making Sofia prior art
Thus, the challenged claims were not entitled to a priority date earlier than their own filing date of March 28, 2014.
8552: Prior-art status: the Delphi prior invention qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(2) because the Delphi inventors appreciated and reduced to practice an embodiment meeting all claim limitations, so the '844 claim 1 is invalid.
We conclude, however, that substantial evidence supports the finding that Intervenors carried that burden.
8565: Prior-art status: whether the video is disqualified as prior art based on applicants' argument of earlier constructive reduction to practice; court held irrelevant under post-AIA first-to-file regime.

Even if appellants were able to show an earlier conception or an earlier constructive reduction to practice, such a showing would be irrelevant to the inquiry required under post-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)
8690: Priority: Agilent proved actual reduction to practice (June 1, 2007) and conception before Dionex's earliest conception date, so Agilent is entitled to priority; substantial evidence supported corroboration under the rule of reason.
The Board did not err in awarding priority to Agilent.
8734: Whether the Tsang reference qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), i.e., whether the relied-upon portions were described 'by another'; the court held the relevant teachings were not 'by another' and so not prior art
We affirm the Board's holdings that arguments as to Okada were untimely and that relevant teachings in Tsang were not "by another."
8778: Whether Alexander qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)(2) despite later cancellation of its claims after IPR; court held it is prior art because the statute requires only that the patent be granted.
The statute does not require that the patent be currently valid.
8841: Whether Itou (U.S. Patent 7,736,355) qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e); the court affirmed that the '116 patent is entitled to the earlier constructive reduction to practice date, so Itou is not prior art.
we affirm the Board's finding of constructive reduction to practice and do not reach the issue of actual reduction to practice.
8871: Prior-art status of Edmondson: Merck antedated Edmondson by reducing the claimed 1:1 (R)-sitagliptin DHP salt to practice before its publication, so Edmondson was only a pre-AIA 102(e) reference and the 103(c)(1) common-ownership exception applied to claims 1, 2, 17, 19, and 21-23.
We agree with Merck that the Board's antedation determination was supported by substantial evidence.
9378: Whether Kovatch qualifies as prior art, given Parus's antedating (prior conception and reduction to practice) showing that the Board declined to consider.
we affirm the Board's holding that Kovatch qualifies as prior art to the challenged patents under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a).
9380: Whether Kurganov-262 qualifies as prior art because the challenged claims are not entitled to the earlier priority date.
we affirm the Board's holding that Kurganov-262 qualifies as prior art to the challenged patents under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a).
9491: Pre-AIA on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b): the Bitelli SF 102 C machine was on sale in this country before the critical date, so it qualifies as prior art against claim 28.

Here, there is substantial evidence to support the Commission's finding that the sale documented by the June 1999 invoice constituted "commercial activity directed to the United States," J.A. 118, namely that the Bitelli SF 102 C machine was sold to a United States customer for use in this country.
9502: Whether Myers qualifies as prior art to claims 1-5, 7 and 9-14 based on the effective filing date of the claims.
The Board thus had substantial evidence on which to base its conclusion that the '571 application did not provide written description support for claims 1, 7, and 12.
9694: Whether the '907 patent claims are entitled to the earlier filing date of the '280 application, so that the ElAttrache publication is prior art; Board found the intervening '707 application lacks written description and cuts off priority.

Accordingly, the Board concluded that the effective filing date of the challenged claims is the filing date of the application that issued as the '907 patent, well after ElAttrache's publication date.
9755: Whether the SMCII qualifies as prior art (on-sale bar before Ridge's critical date); court found corroboration legally sufficient but held credibility and authenticity are for the factfinder, so no ruling on prior-art status.
Before the anticipation issue presented in this case can be resolved, a factfinder will have to evaluate the credibility and persuasiveness of the evidence of corroboration
9820: Prior-art range overlap analysis (prior-art-range cases); court held substantial evidence supported finding that prior-art general working conditions did not overlap the claimed range, so prior-art ranges did not render claims obvious.
Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the general working conditions disclosed in the prior art did not encompass the claimed invention, i.e., there was no overlap in ranges.
10035: Whether the Exhibit (Burns article printout) qualifies as a printed publication and prior art under AIA 102(a)(1); the court held it was publicly accessible by October 20, 2010 and is prior art.

We conclude that Valve established by overwhelming evidence that the Exhibit is a copy of an online article that was publicly accessible on October 20, 2010, that the Board could not find otherwise, and therefore the Exhibit is prior art.
10181: Whether the Sourcefire user guide qualified as a printed publication (prior art under pre-AIA 102(a)/(b) and 311(b)) given its cost and limited distribution; the Board found it publicly accessible and the court affirmed.
On this record, we agree with the Board that Sourcefire was publicly accessible and therefore qualifies as a printed publication.
10532: Whether the alleged prior public use of the Accord K device was sufficiently corroborated to qualify as prior art invalidating the '915 patent claims.
We therefore affirm the Commission's final decision adopting the ALJ's findings and conclusions with respect to corroboration.
10731: Entitlement of claims 21-30 of the '844 patent to the earlier priority date of the GB Application; claims not entitled to that date, so Giambattista is prior art.

The Board held that claims 21–30 are not entitled to claim priority to the GB Application because the GB Application does not provide written description support for an internally-threaded piston rod.
10755: Whether the aspheric coefficients in Tada's Table 5 were an obvious typographical or similar error, so that the errant disclosure cannot be relied on as prior art disclosing the claimed lens.

Considering all the evidence before it, the Board reasonably found that Tada's Table 5 includes an obvious error of a typographical or similar nature that would have been apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art, who would have substituted it with the correct information and, thus, that Table 5 cannot be said to disclose a lens that compresses the center of the image and the edges of the image and expands an intermediate zone of the image located between the center and the edges of the image.
10784: IPA's challenge that the version of FIPA97 in evidence was not prior art (corroboration and related issues); Board's determination that it was prior art affirmed
we see no reversible error, based on the standards for corroboration or otherwise, in the Board’s determination that the version of FIPA97 in evidence was prior art.
10785: Whether Clarke, a CD-distributed conference abstract, was a printed publication and thus prior art
Accordingly, we conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that Clarke was publicly available and thus prior art.
10796: On-sale bar: the district court's summary judgment that the Mersin bed on-sale product anticipated the claims under the on-sale bar was vacated because genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the Fusion instructions apply to the Mersin bed and what the photo shows.
Accordingly, summary judgment was improperly granted.
10910: Whether the Martin reference is prior art under pre-AIA 102(a) as work 'by others' because a third author (Dr. Moran) was a joint inventor of the relied-on portions; Board failed to resolve testimonial conflicts, so the prior-art status finding is vacated.

Because the Board failed to resolve fundamental testimonial conflicts in concluding that the relied-upon reference was not prior art, we vacate the decisions and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
10948: On-sale bar: the Equilon sale was commercial rather than primarily experimental, so the experimental-use doctrine does not negate the bar; remanded on the ready-for-patenting prong.
we reverse the district court’s experimental-use determination and vacate its infringement determination with respect to ’629 patent claim 2 and ’302 patent claims 2, 3, and 16.
11072: Prior-art status of the Voswinckel abstracts as printed publications (public accessibility via conference distribution and research aids), including whether the abstract-book theory raised in Liquidia's reply was properly considered
We find that the Board's conclusion that the Voswinckel abstracts were sufficiently disseminated such that each constituted a printed publication was supported by substantial evidence.
11095: Whether JCT-VC input documents Park and Zhou were publicly accessible and thus qualify as printed publications (prior art) under §102.

In sum, we hold that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that persons of ordinary skill in video-coding technology could have accessed Park and Zhou with reasonable diligence through the JCT-VC organization.
11097: Whether the display of the 'Cherry Star' plant at the Home Depot event was an invalidating prior public use under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), making the claims anticipated (claims 1-4, 6, 7, 11).
The displaying of 'Cherry Star' at the Home Depot event was therefore undoubtedly a use for its intended purpose: ornament.
11162: Whether Shelton I qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102(e) against proposed substitute claims 20 and 21, given the joint-inventorship (by another) analysis under Duncan.
we reverse the Board’s finding that Shelton I constitutes § 102(e) prior art that anticipates proposed substitute claims 20 and 21.
11327: Whether Song '656 and Song '525 are prior art given inventor-origin exception of 102(b)(2); held the exception does not apply to references cited under 102(a)(1)
However, § 102(b)(2) can only disqualify prior art cited under § 102(a)(2).
11368: Prior-art status: exclusion of the Chinook offer document as an on-sale bar (more than one year before filing) was error of law; document should be admitted for obviousness.

Therefore, we reverse the district court's exclusion of the Chinook Document, vacate the judgment that the claims of the '956 patent are not invalid, and remand for a new trial on obviousness based on the on-sale bar.
11454: Priority date in the CRISPR interference: whether Regents' conception and P1/P2 filing dates were entitled to an earlier date. The Board's conception analysis applied the wrong legal standard, so the court vacated and remanded.
We hold that the Board incorrectly applied the legal standard for conception.
11571: Whether published application Lettich is entitled to its provisional filing date as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e); the Board's test was wrong, and the court vacated and remanded for the Board to check support for the specific disclosures relied on.

Because the Board did not, in the first instance, complete this analysis as to whether Lettich qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(e), we vacate and remand for the Board to determine whether the Lettich Provisional Application provides written description support for the specific disclosures in Lettich that the Examiner identified and relied on in the prior art rejections.
11572: Whether pre-AIA 102(e) as amended by the 2002 TAA applies to the pending application; held that it applies, so Lettich may be prior art under the revised statute.
The Examiner and the Board correctly recognized that pre-AIA § 102(e), as revised by the TAA, applies to all patents and applications pending on, or filed after, November 29, 2000.
11644: Whether Cline may be considered as background knowledge of skilled artisan; Board refused to consider it as prior art supplying a missing limitation; affirmed on substantial evidence
We see no error in the Board's treatment of Cline.
11718: Prior-art status under AIA 102(d)(2): whether Carrier's published reference qualifies as prior art as of its provisional filing date. The court held that entitlement to the provisional date requires §112(a) written description support for at least one published claim, rejecting the Board's ministerial-requirements standard, and vacated and remanded.
Accordingly, to establish Carrier as prior art to the ’409 patent, Align must show that Carrier’s provisional application provides written description support for at least one claim of Carrier.
11860: Whether Mann qualifies as analogous art (and thus as prior art) under the field-of-endeavor test; the Board found Mann non-analogous and the court affirmed.

Based on the record before us, we hold that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the field of endeavor of the '924 patent is computer devices that optically sense human input using one or more cameras.
11869: Whether the claimed radiographic letters/identifiable features are printed matter entitled to patentable weight, so they cannot distinguish prior art; treated as a patentable-weight question affecting anticipation.

the district court correctly determined that the claimed "identifiable feature[s]" and "radiographic marker" require nothing more than a radiographically discernible feature, and further that "radiographic letters" are printed matter not entitled to patentable weight
12219: Prior-art status: the August 2012 TCO sale of the TDP-PO tool to Apache, and Apache's use, held to be prior art as a matter of law because the earlier AirLock sale to Tundra was not a public disclosure under section 102(b)(1)(B) (Sanho).
the TDP-PO tool from TCO's August 2012 sale to Apache, and Apache's use of that device, are prior art to the '445 patent.
12227: Watanabe reference not enabled, so not a prior-art basis for the claim 13 obviousness ground (Micron appeal)
Micron points us to no other evidence that would enable a skilled artisan to make the claimed invention, so that ground must fail.
12546: Priority date: the claimed design is not entitled to the earlier filing date of the '938 utility application, so that application qualifies as prior art.
the Board concluded that the design claimed in the '345 application did not benefit from the '938 application's priority date.
12582: Prior-art status under 35 U.S.C. 102(b): the jury instruction on 102(b) was erroneous, so the no-invalidity judgment was vacated and a new trial on invalidity was ordered, following the related Nine Energy opinion.
Accordingly, as in that case, we vacate the judgment of no invalidity and remand for a new trial on invalidity.
12689: Whether IPUG was a printed publication (publicly accessible) qualifying as prior art before the '526 patent's priority date; held prior art.
The Board's determination that IPUG was publicly accessible was supported by substantial evidence.
12741: Priority date: the '583 patent is not entitled to the earlier filing date of the '900 application (Wang '808), so Wang '808 qualifies as prior art because it lacks written description support for 'formed spirally'.
we affirm the Board’s finding that Wang ’808 fails to provide written description support for the claim limitation “formed spirally”
12892: Whether the Aylor references qualify as prior art or whether the '246 application claims are entitled to the earlier priority date; the Board's use of the references as prior art was affirmed because the ADS omitted required application numbers.
Thus, the Board properly affirmed the Examiner's use of the Aylor references as prior art.
12921: Prior-art status and priority date: whether Janevski qualifies as prior art given claimed earlier conception/reduction to practice inuring to inventors' benefit; court did not reach merits of antedating because forfeiture was dispositive.
Because forfeiture is an independent ground for affirmance, we need not and do not reach Implicit's arguments regarding judicial estoppel and waiver.
12923: Prior-art status: whether Bushee is prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) given the patent owner's earlier conception date (antedating via corroborated conception and reasonably continuous diligence)

Taking "all pertinent evidence" into consideration, Fleming, 774 F.3d at 1377, the Board's finding that the Disclosure Documents and the disclosure metadata provide "separate corroboration" for the statements in the Tsaparas Declaration is supported by substantial evidence, Decision at 18.
12924: Diligence: whether the inventors exercised reasonably continuous diligence from just before Bushee's filing date to constructive reduction to practice, supporting antedating of Bushee

In sum, the Board's determination that Valtrus "demonstrated diligence from just prior to Bushee's filing date until a constructive reduction to practice on August 27, 2001," Decision at 22, is supported by substantial evidence.
13323: Prior-art status: Board properly found Bodor is prior art because the seven-line disclosure was not by another inventive entity (complete identity of inventive entity required under Land); patentee failed to show non-prior-art status.
Because Bodor is prior art based on our analysis in Hopewell, and because we see no legal or factual errors in the Board's analysis in this case, we affirm.
13385: Published U.S. patent application (Martin) qualifies as prior art as of its filing date under 102(e)(1) in an IPR, even though it was published after the challenged patent's priority date.
Therefore, Martin, having been filed before the '400 patent's priority date, is a prior art printed publication as to the '400 patent.
13391: Priority date: whether the '953 patent is entitled to the earlier provisional filing date; court held the provisional lacked written description support, so the later date applies and Pfizer's intervening disclosure is prior art.

The '048 provisional did not disclose —NHC(O)—C1-alkyl. It therefore provided no written description support for the '953 patent, so the '953 patent cannot be afforded the '048 provisional's priority date.
13496: Whether Pioneer Hi-Bred is an enabling prior-art reference (enablement of the anticipatory disclosure); affirmed as enabling.
For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the Board's determination that Pioneer Hi-Bred's disclosure is enabling.
13663: Whether Maninis qualifies as prior art because it was publicly accessible before the prior art date; the Board's finding was upheld.
substantial evidence supports the Board’s conclusion that Maninis was publicly accessible before the prior art date
13668: Prior-art status and priority date: whether Wu is prior art, i.e., whether the patentee swore behind Wu by establishing an earlier actual reduction to practice (corroborated inventor testimony).
Moreover, the Board did not err in its ultimate determination that Shenzhen had not met its burden of proving that Wu was prior art with respect to the '555 patent.
13790: Whether the '625 patent is entitled to the April 2, 2004 Korean application priority date; the Korean application does not disclose E-AGCH or absolute grants, so the 3GPP references qualify as prior art.
For that reason, the ’625 patent is not entitled to the filing date of that application and the 3GPP References qualify as prior art.
13810: Whether the Bodor six-line disclosure, filed by a subset of the inventors, is prior art under pre-AIA 102(a) and (e) ('by another') against the patents-in-suit, including the burden of production.
we hold that the Board did not legally or factually err in holding that the six-line disclosure was prior art as to the patents-in-suit.
13838: Pre-AIA on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b): the court held the letter to Complete was a commercial offer for sale made in this country before the critical date, so the asserted claims are invalid as prior art.
the asserted claims of the asserted patents are invalid under § 102(b), and we reverse the district court's judgment and remand for entry of judgment in Belvac's favor.
14233: Prior-art status under §102(b)(2)(B): whether the inventor's private, non-confidential sale of the HyperDrive publicly disclosed the subject matter so that Kuo is not prior art; court held the sale was not a public disclosure and Kuo is prior art.
We conclude that the sale of the HyperDrive here did not publicly disclose the subject matter relied on from Kuo as required by section 102(b)(2)(B).
14254: Whether the PP3 sold before the critical date qualifies as prior art under the on-sale bar despite lack of disclosure of the inner workings of the device
triggering the on-sale bar does not "require that the sale make the details of the invention available to the public."
14278: Whether RadioShack web manual was publicly accessible and thus prior art under 102 (printed publication).
Because those findings were supported by substantial evidence, we agree that RadioShack is available as prior art under § 102.
14337: Prior-art status of the DiskOnKey Firmware Upgrader under the pre-AIA public use bar; substantial evidence supported finding it was in public use before the critical date, so it is prior art.
Because substantial evidence supports the jury's verdict finding that the Firmware Upgrader was in public use, we affirm.
14521: Priority date: '039 patent not entitled to 2004 application date, so Enhertu's 2015 disclosure is prior art that anticipates
The '039 patent thus cannot claim priority from the 2004 application, meaning that the December 2015 public disclosure of Enhertu ... anticipates, and thus invalidates the '039 patent.
14523: On-sale bar under AIA §102(a)(1): whether Celanese's pre-critical-date sales of Ace-K made using its secret process are prior art that invalidates the asserted process claims. Court held the AIA did not change the pre-AIA rule, so the sales bar patentability.
Celanese's pre-2015 sales of Ace-K made using its secret process thus trigger the on-sale bar and preclude patentability of that process.
14713: Whether Cranley, a published patent application, qualifies as prior art; the Rule 131 prior-invention affidavit does not apply to a statutory-bar rejection based on a published reference.
Therefore, because the earliest priority date of Haines's application is October 29, 2009, ... Cranley was properly determined to be prior art.
15141: On-sale bar (AIA 102) for the '125 and '540 tube patents: court held Dr. Lebby's testimony alone insufficient to show prior art tubes were on sale, but reversed JMOL of no invalidity and ordered new trial on validity.
the district court did not err in concluding that Dr. Lebby's testimony alone did not suffice to establish that the prior art tubes were on sale before the tube patents' effective filing dates.
15149: Priority date: the '912 patent is not entitled to the earlier priority dates of the '436 patent and '244 provisional, so the later date applies and Ellsberry is prior art.
Substantial evidence supports that finding as well.
15264: Whether Tian qualifies as analogous prior art (reasonably pertinent to the problem the inventor faced); Board found Tian analogous and court affirmed.
We conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's reasonable-pertinence finding and its determination that Tian is analogous art.
15277: Whether iRobot swore behind Jeon and Abramson by proving prior conception corroborated by independent evidence, so that the references are prior art under pre-AIA 102(e).

We therefore affirm the Board’s ultimate determination that iRobot did not successfully swear behind Jeon and Abramson and that therefore those references were available as prior art to assert against the ’423 patent.
